title: Max Partitions After One Change
statement:
You are given a string `S` of lowercase English letters and an integer `K`.

An **operation** removes the **longest prefix** of the current string that contains **at most `K` distinct characters**. The remaining characters (possibly none) form the string for the next operation. You repeat operations until the string is empty. Since `K ≥ 1`, every operation removes at least one character.

Before performing any operation you may change **at most one** character of `S` to any lowercase English letter (or leave `S` as it is).

Return the **maximum number of operations** that can be performed.
inputFormat:
The first line contains the string `S`.
The second line contains the integer `K`.
outputFormat: Print a single integer: the maximum possible number of operations.

examples.explanation: Without a change the whole string has only 3 distinct letters, so a single operation removes everything. Changing `S[3]` to `z` gives `abczcba`: the first operation removes `abc` (adding `z` would make 4 distinct letters), the second removes `zcb`, the third removes `a`. That is 3 operations.
The string has only 2 distinct letters. Even after changing one character it has at most 3, so the first operation always removes the whole string.

With `K = 1` every operation removes a run of equal letters. Without a change: `aa`, then `b`, that is 2 operations. Changing `S[1]` to `c` gives `acb`, which splits into `a`, `c`, `b`: 3 operations. A string of length 3 cannot give more.

hints: Greedy partitioning of a fixed string is easy to simulate in O(n). The difficulty is the single change: trying every position and every letter is too slow.

Fix the position `i` you change. The prefix before `i` and the suffix after `i` can each be summarised by (completed operations, set of letters in the unfinished piece). Precompute these for every `i`, using bitmasks for the letter sets.

Look at how the changed character interacts with the two unfinished pieces: it can be merged with both into one operation, make a new operation by itself (needs a letter not in either piece, both pieces already at `K` letters), or be absorbed on one side. Take the best over all positions.
